abstract: The evolutionarily conserved insulin/IGF-1 signalling pathway (IIS) shapes life-history traits largely through downstream transcription factors including SKN-1. Reduced IIS (rIIS) in adulthood robustly extends Caenorhabditis elegans lifespan, yet developmental rIIS has long been considered unable to extend lifespan and costly to fitness, a conclusion drawn almost entirely from experiments at 25{degrees}C, near the species' upper thermal limit. Here we knocked down daf-2 during development in wild-type and skn-1 loss-of-function nematodes across constant and fluctuating temperatures. Contrary to the prevailing view, developmental daf-2 knockdown extended lifespan at constant 15{degrees}C in both backgrounds, but not at 25{degrees}C, revealing that its late-life benefit is strongly temperature-dependent and, under constant conditions, independent of skn-1. Under daily 15-25{degrees}C cycling, developmental daf-2 knockdown again extended lifespan, but whether this required skn-1 was itself determined by the temperature experienced at the start of development. Lifespan extension was accompanied by condition-specific reproductive costs. Together, our results identify a developmental window in which IIS, skn-1 and temperature interact to set adult ageing trajectories and show that the thermal environment determines whether reducing IIS during development extends lifespan.
